newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE SLAMS ATHLETICS CHIEF NEBIOLO FOR COMMENTS.
newsitem.headline: GREECE SLAMS ATHLETICS CHIEF NEBIOLO FOR COMMENTS.

text.p: Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos joined a chorus of angry Greek reaction against world athletics chief Primo Nebiolo on Tuesday, saying the Italian lawyer was uninformed and should keep out of politics.

Seen as an enemy of Athens's bid to host the 2004 Olympics, also sought by Rome and three other cities, Nebiolo told Greek television that the Games will not solve Greece's political and economic problems.

"Mr. Nebiolo committed a gross violation of a very basic rule," the outspoken Pangalos told reporters. "Politicians are allowed to speak about sports but sports officials are not allowed to speak about politics."

The head of the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), which held its world championship in Athens last week, prompted a fresh storm of reaction in Greece after comments to the private Mega television channel on Monday evening.
"You have many problems, economic, political...(problems) with the Maastricht treaty, the value of money and unemployment. and the Olympic Games will not solve these problems," he told Mega.
Greek newspapers lashed out at Nebiolo in front-page banner headlines, calling him "Mafioso", "Duce" and a shameless advocate of Rome's bid to host the Games.

Rome and Athens are the favourites among the five bidding cities, especially after the explosion which on Friday destroyed sections of the Olympic stadium in Stockholm, the third European candidate. Cape Town and Buenos Aires are the other bidding cities who learn their fate in Lausanne on September 5.
Athens' bid hinged on a well-run championships. A nearly empty stadium on the first weekend was an embarrassment to organisers who blamed it on the long duration of the event and expensive tickets.
Nebiolo was quick to criticise both Greek organisers and the public. His comments prompted a flurry of reaction and he was greeted with loud boos at the closing ceremony on Sunday.

"There has maybe not been a great campaign of promotion," Nebiolo had said. "Maybe because it was Saturday people in Athens go to the sea...they have the sea all year. They can forget the sea for a week."

Seats were promptly filled out and observers praised the event's efficiency. Nebiolo told Mega the success of the championships was mainly owed to IAAF and not Greek organisers, whom he described as "mediocre".
Athens Mayor Dimitris Avramopoulos and Greek Olympic Committee head Lambis Nicolaou accused Nebiolo of painting Greece as a troubled nation to promote Rome's Olympic candidacy.
Pangalos said that Nebiolo was "not well informed" about Greece and lashed back, describing Italy as a country that faces security problems because of the mafia.
"Italy uses its armed forces to deal with the terrifying problem of the mafia, which it exports to the rest of the world, like the United States and recently Albania," he said.
"But I would never say that the mafia characterises Italy and therefore Rome does not deserve the Games. Rome will not win the Games simply because Athens is better," he added.
